text: nature reviews genetics https://doi.org/10.1038/s41576-023-00671-0 Perspective Check for updates Translating genomic advances into biodiversity conservation A key action of the new Global Biodiversity Framework is the maintenance of genetic diversity in all species to safeguard their adaptive potential. To achieve this goal, a translational mindset, which aims to convert results of basic research into direct practical benefits, needs to be applied to biodiversity conservation. Despite much discussion on the value of genomics to conservation, a disconnect between those generating genomic resources and those applying it to biodiversity management remains. As global efforts to generate reference genomes for non-model species increase, investment into practical biodiversity applications is critically important. Applications such as understanding population and multispecies diversity and longitudinal monitoring need support alongside education for policymakers on integrating the data into evidence-based decisions. Without such investment, the opportunity to revolutionize global biodiversity conservation using genomics will not be fully realized.

text: The year 2023 marked the 20th anniversary of the publication of the human reference genome7. Since then, investment into genomic applications has revolutionized the practice of human medicine (reviewed, for example, in refs. 8–10), creating new financial opportunities for technological advancements11 and informing numerous aspects of public health policy10. This technological revolution has also provided the opportunity to investigate and understand the diversity of genes across all species in a more cost-effective and efficient manner12 and to measure and implement a key goal of conservation policy: having large enough populations to harbour sufficient genetic variation so as to be resilient in an ever-changing world13. The field of conservation genetics, defined as the use of genetics to aid in the conservation of small populations or species, has been around for decades14, yet in the past few years, there has been much commentary in the scientific literature on the value of genomics to conservation management (reviewed, for example, in refs. A key review published in 2010 (ref. 18) has succinctly identified a Introduction Biodiversity is critically important for human food security and health, as well as planetary survival1. However, the planet is in a biodiversity crisis, with the ongoing sixth mass extinction event being attributed to anthropogenic drivers2. A recent study has shown that more than 32% of 27,000 vertebrate species have declining populations3, whereas insect populations have decreased by an average of 37% over the past 30 years4,5. Biodiversity, as defined by the Convention of Biological Diversity (first signed at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit by 150 countries), includes three pillars: “the genetic level (i.e., the richness of genetically different types within the total population), species level (i.e., the richness of species in an area), and ecosystem level (i.e., the richness of ecosystem types within a given area)”6. For close to 100 years, biologists have been furthering their understanding of two of these pillars (ecosystems and species) but limited technological capacity has prevented the thorough investigation of the third pillar (gene diversity).

These types of frameworks will be critical moving forward. In December 2022, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework was signed by 188 of the 196 parties to the United Nations Convention of Biological Diversity29. Maintenance of genetic diversity and the benefit sharing of genetic resources are key aspects to both the 2030 targets and 2050 goals29. Here I present a brief history of genomics in conservation policy and the research–implementation gap, synthesizing the range of newly published workflows. This is not a comprehensive review of the science of conservation genomics, but rather a discussion of what has been achieved, what still needs attention and how investment is needed to move the field into translational science to ensure that the latest basic research and technology is applied into practical conservation actions.

text: Status of genomics in conservation policy In the conservation policy arena, the Global Biodiversity Framework recognizes the value of maintaining and restoring genetic diversity within, and between, populations to maintain their adaptive potential29. To achieve this goal, genomic data is needed to inform a range of biodiversity conservation actions including, but not limited to, determining species taxonomy30, assessing species at risk31, informing management strategies for both in situ populations (those in their natural state in their natural habitat) and ex situ populations (those outside their natural habitat)32, and monitoring changes and/or benefits in systems as conservation interventions occur33. It has recently been highlighted that genomic data is not used to its full potential in conservation practice because of the ongoing debate surrounding genetic metrics and how to measure genetic health to inform policy decisions28,34. This issue is compounded by the research–implementation gap between specialists who generate (genome biologists and geneticists) and analyse (bioinformaticians) complex datasets and those who work at the biodiversity conservation coalface who need to implement the results of the data to inform their conservation management actions (ecologists and conservation practitioners) and their decision-making (policy advisers and legislators)20. The many proposed causes and solutions for addressing the conservation genetics research–implementation gap (see Box 1) are not the focus of this Perspective. Rather, it is the accumulation of scientific information and knowledge and the lack of investment to be able to easily translate scientific advances into management actions and relevant legislation that is of concern35.

text: Tools for applying genomic resources The field of biodiversity genomics for conservation applications has benefited from the technological advances of human genomics and The term ‘research–implementation gap’144 has been used to describe the gap between research outputs and their uptake into applied management actions. It is not a new concept, dating back to the early establishment of the field of conservation biology145. It has been identified in a range of conservation-related fields such as conservation genetics20, invasion biology35 and ecology146. The reasons behind the existence of research–implementation gap are wide and varied, including lack of interdisciplinary collaboration35, a perceived lack of expertise within practitioner groups20, usefulness and access of scientific literature to practitioners35 and lack of funding20. In conservation-related fields, it has been suggested that the terminology ‘research–implementation’ fails to acknowledge that many practitioners and policymakers are scientists who work in government and/or other conservation agencies rather than academia21. Moreover, the use of the word ‘gap’ implies a void that needs to be filled23. It has, therefore, been proposed that the challenges facing researchers and conservation practitioners would be more accurately described as co-existing within a series of productive ‘spaces’; the focus then shifts to how academic researchers and conservation partners could work in collaboration to identify knowledge gaps and co-design ways to fill them23. Within each space, there are shared interests, different values and/or drivers, and complex relationships between research academics and practitioners that need to be acknowledged and addressed23. It has been proposed that these spaces are wider in fields such as biodiversity genomics, in which high-end specialist skills are needed to generate, analyse and interpret big genomic datasets78. Many of these high-end specialist skills tend not to be found within practice-focused institutions, thereby requiring practitioners to partner with research-focused organizations to generate the data needed for management actions. However, the priorities and norms of research-focused and practice-focused institutions often differ, resulting in different performance requirements and leading to institutional mismatches and potential conflict21. In some instances, those with high-end specialist skills are employed in practice-focused institutions; however, they tend to work on species of high economic value in well-resourced regions of the world rather than on species of conservation concern51, which are often found in under-resourced regions. Although progress is being made, it is not occurring at the same rate globally. research into model and agricultural species36, many of which are eutherian mammals or species that have been line-bred for specific genetic benefits (such as cattle, chickens, wheat and soy). A high number of these advances, particularly in relation to extraction and sequencing of DNA and RNA, are translatable to biodiversity genomics and the plethora of species that exist on the planet. However, some current methods encounter problems with the genomes of non-model species owing to features such as polyploidy37, parthenogenesis38, cytogenomic architecture39 and the vast differences in genome sizes; some eukaryotic species have small (<1 Gb) genomes, such as the 0.061 Gb of the carnivorous plant Genlisea tuberosa40, whereas others range from medium (3–4 Gb) to gigantic, such as the Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba), a small invertebrate species which, at just 6 cm in length, has a genome size of 48.01 Gb (ref. 41) (25 times larger than the human genome). Moreover, many analytical pipelines, algorithms and chemistries that were developed for generating reference genomes for humans and model species are sometimes unable to cope with the diverse genomes of non-model species, which exhibit large variations in genome size40,41, chromosome number and chromosome length42, to name a few. Although a reference genome has no direct impact on conservation outcomes24, it provides the foundational blueprint for a suite of downstream applications (Fig. 1), including understanding functional diversity within a species or ecosystem, and enhancing our understanding of adaptive potential, which is critical in a changing climate and on a planet where population fragmentation is increasing owing to anthropogenic factors2. Thus, since the late 2000s, a range of global genome consortia have been established to develop reference genomes for non-model species including genomes within taxa (for example, Bird10K (ref. 43) and Bat1K (ref. 44)) or groups of taxa (for example, the 10K genomes project45 and Vertebrate Genome Project46) and, in 2018, the Earth Biogenome Project was launched with the ambitious aim of sequencing all eukaryotic life on Earth over a 10-year period in a series of stages19. Although these global consortia are developing single reference genome assemblies at a rapid rate (which can be monitored in real time at Genomes on a Tree), less than 1% of the approximately 35,500 species listed as threatened (critically endangered, endangered and vulnerable) under the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) have published genomic resources47. However, this figure is anticipated to change in the coming 5-year period as initiatives such as the California Conservation Genomics Project48,49, Threatened Species Initiative24 and European Reference Genome Atlas50 generate genomic resources for species of conservation concern (Box 2). Moreover, the investment into generating reference genomes for large numbers of non-model species by these consortia is providing regular advances that should reduce some of the current analysis and computational issues surrounding the use of non-model species genomes12. In addition to developing reference genome assemblies, some projects, such as the California Conservation Genomics Project and the Threatened Species Initiative, are also generating population genomic resources that are quantifying the amount and distribution of within-species genomic diversity, which is needed for conservation management decisions and policy. These projects not only develop peer-reviewed scientific publications but also generate reports for the relevant conservation or government agencies that include a list of recommended management actions based on the genomic resources. However, for these recommendations to be implemented, these agencies need to employ personnel with the ability to interpret, understand and integrate genomic data into their management action frameworks. This means that investment is needed to embed scientists with high-end specialist skills in biodiversity genomics into management and policy agencies. A recent systematic review highlighted that this is particularly important for species of conservation concern, as high-end specialists are often already employed by agencies managing species of economic or commercial value, such as fisheries, particularly in regions such as North America and Europe51. A combination of long-read genome sequencing and transcriptomes for non-model species allows for species-specific annotations of the genome, as automated pipelines have difficulty in annotating gene expansions, or complex gene families in evolutionarily distinct species42. Once annotated, a range of downstream genomic tools can be developed using both neutral and functional markers to investigate a range of biological and conservation-related questions. Current PacBio High Fidelity long-read sequencing also permits the organelle genome to be assembled bioinformatically, reducing the need for further sequencing143 and permitting the development of species-specific metabarcodes for addressing questions pertaining to taxonomic resolution and environmental DNA (eDNA). to develop a range of tools and workflows in the lead up to the new Global Biodiversity Framework by a number of working groups. These include the Society of Conservation Biology Conservation Genetics Working Group (SCB CGWG), Genomic Biodiversity Knowledge for Resilient Ecosystems (G-BIKE), IUCN Species Survival Commission Conservation Genetics Specialist Group (IUCN-SSC CGSG), Group on Earth Observations Biodiversity Network Genetic Composition Working Group (GEOBON GCWG) and the development of the Coalition of Conservation Geneticists26. The objective of these working groups has been to develop a series of globally recognized consistent indicators (genetic Essential Biodiversity Variables (EBVs)) (Box 3) for assessing genetic diversity and for reporting on these for the Global Biodiversity Framework52,53. In addition to these indicators, different workflows have been published on implementing genetic tools into conservation practice13,25,27,28,48,54 (Fig. 2). Evidence-based decision tools have also been developed, such as the UK-based Conservation Evidence Initiative, to assist policymakers and managers in how to incorporate diverse types of evidence into decisions pertaining to management actions including the integration of genomic data55–57. Although these decision tools along with globally recognized indicators (Box 3) lay the groundwork for the ongoing use of genomic tools into management, the key variable that is missing is ongoing investment to make these different tools and frameworks an operational reality. Even more critical is the fact that access to genetic sequencing and implementation of genetic data is not equitable across developed and developing economies51,58 (see ‘Equitable access’), and five concerns were raised by developing nations during the development of the new Global Biodiversity Framework53. These included the necessity of DNA data, feasibility of obtaining sufficient data, realistic limitations on time, limitations on skills and knowledge, and concerns over data sharing53. To combat these concerns, three indicators for assessing genetic diversity have been proposed. These indicators do not necessarily require new genetic data, are affordable and achievable in the Framework time frames, can be easily translated into policy and management, and can be applied across multiple countries, taxonomic groups and ecosystems. Indicator 1 uses effective population size (Ne) to quantify the rate of genetic erosion in the population, indicator 2 uses the proportion of populations maintained within species, and indicator 3 is the number of species and populations monitored using DNA methods53. These indicators are a stopgap measure that complement other tools for tracking genetic diversity and provide parties to the Global Biodiversity Framework with an immediate and actionable way forward in the absence of access to sequencing and data, giving time for these parties to increase their capacity for long-term genetic monitoring28.

text: Practical and design considerations In addition to equitable and fair access, there are a range of practical and design considerations when applying genomics tools for use in conservation management. Most important is the engagement and communication with Indigenous peoples and local communities to ensure projects are co-designed, sampling is undertaken in a culturally respectful manner, and downstream benefit sharing is negotiated59. Other key considerations include the types of conservation management actions that can be informed by genetic and/or genomic data; cost versus data informativeness; repeatability and reproducibility of the sampling design and application25; whether a reference genome is required for the species, as conspecific, congeneric and confamilial genomes have been shown to be suitable proxies for managing some species of conservation concern60; the ease of access to sequencing58; and the choice of markers to be used, the type of coverage and whether this is suitable for the questions being asked61. There are several unique Examples of projects that are developing genomic data for biodiversity management California Conservation Genomics Project This is a state-based programme in the USA. Commencing in 2019, the CCGP is a US$10 million project led by the University of California Los Angeles (UCLA). It is a consortium of more than 100 conservation scientists from across California. Their objective is to produce the most comprehensive multispecies genomic dataset to help manage and protect regional biodiversity in the face of climate change48,49. As of May 2023, they had 257 species in their programme including invertebrates, plants, marine and terrestrial vertebrate species.

text: Threatened Species Initiative This is a national programme in Australia. Commencing in 2020, the Threatened Species Initiative was awarded US$700,000 (Bioplatforms Australia) and US$335,000 (Australian government). Their objective is to develop genomic resources for some of the most threatened species in Australia, as well as a series of online tools to upskill conservation end users and data analysis tools to produce a standardized conservation report24, reporting on the recommended genetic Essential Biodiversity Variables52. It is a collaborative network encouraging academic researchers and conservation end users to partner together to collect samples, generate data and apply genetic data to management actions. As of May 2023, they had 87 species, including invertebrates, plants, marine and terrestrial species, with over 200 collaborators in the programme.

text: European Reference Genome Atlas This is a multi-national programme in Europe. Commencing in 2021, their objective is to support the sequencing of reference-quality genomes for all European species to inform the protection of European biodiversity50. With seed funding of US$10 million from the European Commission, this is a collaborative interdisciplinary network, connecting the relevant infrastructure across Europe. As of May 2023, they had 630 species included in their programme. considerations when working with threatened species or communities, such as access to suitable samples for reference genomes and samples for transcriptomic data for species-specific gene annotations24. Furthermore, sampling populations of threatened species can be problematic owing to their scarcity or cryptic nature, making population genetic assessments difficult. In addition to all these immediate practical and design considerations, geneticists need to keep in mind how they will ‘future-proof’ the data they generate, whether they undertake whole-genome sequencing of high coverage, or biobank samples for future use62. Although this list of considerations may seem long and complex, when applied correctly, they can have significant conservation benefit (Box 4). New technologies also have scope to change how genetics and genomics are used to inform conservation, including an improved ability to use historical museum collections63 and environmental DNA (eDNA)64 to increase our understanding of biodiversity. Natural history museum collections hold over 1.1 billion objects65 whose genomes can now be accessed using new extraction methods and applications of genetic sequencing, allowing us to understand how biodiversity has changed over the past few hundred years. Ancient DNA methods are improving each year, permitting us to investigate changes that occurred in populations that went extinct in the past few decades (such as the thylacine, Thylacinus cynocephalus66), hundreds of years ago (such as Steller’s sea cow, Hydrodamalis gigas67) and even thousands of years ago (such as the woolly mammoth, Mammuthus primigenius68). The linking of genomics to morphology using global museum collections is emerging as a previously untapped resource in our understanding of global biodiversity. Historical DNA techniques and museum specimens collected prior to the large-scale declines allow us to detect and understand temporal and spatial genomic erosion69,70, which informs our interpretation of modern-day low genetic diversity and its relevance to conserving species70. However, before these resources can be utilized, the Indigenous peoples and local communities from which these collections came must be consulted: otherwise, we will simply perpetuate the actions of our colonial past59. Analysis of eDNA using a range of environmental sources, including water64, soil64 and air71 samples, is already used to inform actions pertaining to biosecurity72 and is proving to be a useful tool for assessing the presence of species that are either cryptic or difficult to detect. Moving forward, the simplicity of collecting samples and sequencing for eDNA will make this an exceedingly useful technology for developing nations to start to understand and generate data for the protection of their local biodiversity73.

text: Future perspectives Academic research efforts of the past decade have greatly advanced our ability to use genomic data to understand biodiversity (Table 1), and global efforts have now developed a range of frameworks and workflows so this genomic data can be applied (Fig. 2). There will always be research questions that use genomic tools to understand global biodiversity; but ongoing discussions of the value of genomics to conservation management need to end and the tools that have been developed need to simply be applied — this requires both translational investment and equitable access to fully realize the benefits of genomic tools for biodiversity protection.

text: Equitable access There are 17 megadiverse nations — countries that harbour 60–80% of global biodiversity74. However, access to sequencing technology, bioinformatic expertise and conservation funding is not equitable across these nations. Only two of the 17 nations — USA and Australia — are developed economies with annual gross domestic product (GDP) per capita of US$65,000 and US$54,800, respectively; by contrast, the remaining 15 nations each has a GDP per capita of less than US$16,000 (ref. Although the new Global Biodiversity Framework has a goal associated with benefit sharing of genetic resources29, implementation of the FAIR principles (findability, accessibility, interoperability and reusability) Four genetic Essential Biodiversity Variables have been proposed for monitoring genetic diversity under the Global Biodiversity Framework52: intraspecific genetic diversity, genetic differentiation, inbreeding and effective population size. The descriptions provided below have been paraphrased from Hoban et al.52. 1. Genetic diversity: the amount of genetic variability within a species or population that contributes to its adaptive potential and likelihood of persistence. Two components are proposed, both of which should be recorded to fully capture genetic diversity: a. Richness — the number of genetic variants within a population of a species, accounting for differences in sample sizes b. Evenness — characterized by expected heterozygosity (He) and is the probability that any two random alleles selected from a sample are not the same 2. Genetic differentiation: the differences in allelic frequencies between multiple populations of a species, caused by limited gene flow, natural selection and genetic drift. Two components have been proposed: a. Number of genetic units or lineages across the species range b. Degree of differentiation among the populations or genetic units 3. Inbreeding: the degree to which a pair of individuals is related, mating between relatives occurs, or two individuals share identity by descent. It is used to assess genetic diversity within individuals. 4. Effective population size (Ne): a way to quantify current genetic change and predict future changes owing to genetic drift. It is defined as the number of individuals in a theoretical ideal population in which random mating occurs and a Poissondistributed number of offspring are produced each generation. This ideal population experiences the same magnitude of genetic diversity loss as the real population. and CARE principles (how data should be treated to ensure indigenous governance, that is, collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility and ethics) are key to its success. Adherence to these principles in the biodiversity genomics space is still in its infancy but needs to be addressed as a matter of priority59. Globally, there has been a recent transition to include Indigenous knowledge and engagement in the management of biodiversity, in part­ icular in the use of genetic resources59. Partnerships with Indigenous peoples and local communities permit those who have connection to the species to have ownership over the data produced59,75. Genomic technologies rapidly advance and change each year, and although many groups outside of North America and Europe have the desire to use the latest technology, it is either too expensive or is not provided within their countries58. The solution to this problem in the past has been for scientists and conservation managers residing in countries without sequencing access to send samples to those nations that do have access to sequencing capacity (for example, North America, Europe, China or Singapore). Yet, this is in contradiction to the accessibility (under FAIR) and the collective benefit and the authority to control (under CARE) principles that underpin the Global Biodiversity Framework. If we are to fully utilize the benefits of genomic technologies for the management of biodiversity, then equitable access to sequencing, bioinformatics and funding needs to be addressed58. Addressing funding and use of genetic data for biodiversity management is also encompassed in the new Global Biodiversity Framework29. However, equitable access to sequencing technology will require major sequencing companies to engage with developing economies to find economical solutions for sequencing access; both Illumina and Oxford Nanopore Technology have made pledges to this effect. Investment into bioinformatics capacity and education also needs to be improved globally to ensure that scientists and conservation managers without in-country sequencing access can still use available genetic datasets that are generated for their species of interest. Scientists, journal editors and funding agencies in developed economies have a responsibility to advance tools and methodologies that permit easier access for those residing in developing nations. Providing open-source cloud-based tools for analysing genetic and genomic datasets would enable those who do not have the capacity or the computing infrastructure to generate sequence data, to analyse available datasets and to apply the results to their within-country biodiversity management actions24.

As discussed, the space between research and implementation in the conservation-genomics area is widening by different degrees across the world. The reasons are varied but include the ever-increasing development in sequencing technology and biotechnology36, the increase in bioinformatic complexity and computational requirements78, and the need for fundamental research into our biological understanding of genomic data and how it will inform conservation policy and management. Integrating genetic management theory, genomic methods and bioinformatic tools (for example, basic command line, standard Examples of projects in which genetic data have improved conservation efforts Scimitar-horned oryx Last seen in the wild in the late 1980s to early 1990s, the scimitar-horned oryx (Oryx dammah) is a conservation success story. About 48–60 oryx were collected from the wild between 1937 and 1967 with approximately 23,000 oryx in the ex situ population today147. Over a 10-year period, three empirical genetic datasets were generated for this species: mitochondrial DNA, nuclear microsatellite and single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) markers133. This data was used to characterize the genetic diversity of the ex situ population to ascertain the best source populations for the reintroduction programme of oryx back into Chad that commenced in 2016 (ref. 148). The population now exceeds 400 free-roaming oryx149. This project strongly demonstrates the value of genetic data in ensuring that oryx in the reintroduction project represent the greatest breadth of evolutionary potential for the long-term survival of the species133. A chromosome-length assembly genome150, and associated resequenced genomes151, have greatly improved our understanding of the impacts of inbreeding and mutational load in this species, and informed management strategies for oryx and other threatened species (see the figure, part a; image courtesy of Tania Gilbert, Marwell Wildlife).

text: Tasmanian devil Tasmanian devils (Sarcophilus harrisii) are endangered owing to an infectious clonal cancer, the devil facial tumour disease, that has resulted in a more than 80% decline in the species across their range105. A wide range of genetic datasets have been generated for this species152, including microsatellites, mitochondrial DNA, amplicons, SNP markers, target-capture methods and whole-genome resequencing. The first reference genome was published in 2012 (ref. 153), permitting the characterization of the disease and the lack of diversity within the immune genes in the devils, a key factor in the disease spread154. An updated chromosome-level genome was published in 2023 (ref. 155), allowing for the development of new methods to investigate the interplay between immune genes and devil facial tumour disease156, and the generation of more informative SNPs to assess genome-wide and functional diversity105. Since 2010, genetic data has been used to manage various aspects of Tasmanian devil populations including relatedness of the insurance population founders132, overall metapopulation management105 and informing translocation decisions157 (see the figure, part b; image courtesy of Carolyn J. text: One suggested pathway for translational investment is through the developing biodiversity markets. Policy and legislation need to recognize the conflict that currently exists between economic growth and biodiversity loss81, and this conflict will need to be resolved if biodiversity markets are to be successful in achieving their goals of protecting nature. The term ‘nature-positive solutions’ is now being commonly used; these are characterized as solutions that will halt and reverse nature loss measured from a baseline of 2020, although this aspirational term is under threat of dilution as there is no consistent globally used definition82. This concept, which has been suggested as a way to increase investment into biodiversity, should be learning from the experiences of the carbon markets; carbon markets developed a series of investment principles around the concept of ‘net zero’ that permitted funds to flow from the corporate sector to the research sector for the development of new tools and technologies to achieve the net-zero goal83. However, a biodiversity market is a harder concept to develop because biodiversity loss, although a global crisis2, tends to be more localized than atmospheric carbon markets. Recently, four key elements were proposed for nature-positive strategies to enable business to undertake transformative action for biodiversity84: positive biodiversity outcomes across the value chain, organizational buy-in, integration of biodiversity and climate, and measurable outcomes against a fixed baseline. In addition, the new Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD) framework has been developed to enable companies and financial institutions to integrate nature into their decision-making and assessment of corporate risk. However, the TNFD still requires companies to be able to identify their impact on nature, mitigate their impact and monitor the effect of their mitigation — all these measures require the ability to measure and monitor biodiversity at scale. Thus, internationally, we need economic solutions for biodiversity markets, whereby generating and housing public data (such as genomic data) for global and societal benefit become an investible biodiversity asset; these assets can be generated, hosted and used to inform management actions and policy development and to provide data access and transparency for business and their biodiversity commitments. Until such an economic solution that provides a pathway for financial investment into translational science for biodiversity conservation can be found, the generation of genomic data that will benefit everyone by informing biodiversity protection and management will remain in the limited arena of academia and research funding.

filename: Hogg 2023_ Translating genomic advances into biodiversity conservation.pdf
text: Conclusions Conservation management actions and associated legislation should be based on the best possible available evidence. There have been sizable efforts by the scientific community in recent years to develop evidence-based decision tools and frameworks for protecting biodiversity, many of which integrate genomic data. However, large-scale investment is the only true way to move the fields of biodiversity and conservation genomics from the academic sector into the applied conservation and policy sectors for biodiversity protection. If nature-positive solutions are to be used to benefit humanity and conserve biodiversity, businesses need to be encouraged to invest in the development and application of technological tools for measuring and monitoring current biodiversity against a fixed baseline. Genomic tools applied at scale can help inform our understanding of the distribution, evolution and adaptive potential of our remaining biodiversity. Although challenges on their implementation remain (namely, equitable access, education for non-specialists and investment to further develop practical applied tools), they are not insurmountable as many genomic tools are already applied at scale in both human health and agriculture. For conservation managers, having genetic data available for biodiversity management is the difference between flying blind or flying with a navigation system. Genetic diversity is one of the key pillars to supporting biodiversity29 and, as our understanding of the value and application of genomic technologies to managing populations and species increases, we find ourselves on the cusp of a new applied biodiversity genomics revolution — one that sees the integration of genomic data into management actions and the legislative policy and financial incentives to support it. However, its success will be dependent on a commitment to and investment into translational science.
